name: Primary Raynaud Phenomenon

criteria.description: Episodic, symmetrical attacks of digital pallor and/or cyanosis triggered by cold or emotional stress
No evidence of secondary cause (no underlying connective tissue disease, occupational exposure, or other associated condition)
No digital pitting, ulceration, or gangrene

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Episodic digital color changes (at least biphasic: pallor and cyanosis, or pallor and rubor) triggered by cold/stress, with no clinical or laboratory evidence of a secondary cause.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Primary Raynaud is diagnosis of exclusion. Must rule out secondary causes (scleroderma, SLE, MCTD, etc.). Nailfold capillaroscopy and ANA are key screening tools for secondary disease.

pathognomonic.notes: Classic triphasic (pallor-cyanosis-rubor) in ~65%; biphasic in remainder

pathognomonic.symptomName: Episodic digital pallor (white) triggered by cold
pathognomonic.notes: Well-demarcated pallor of one or more digits

common.symptomName: Pain in affected digits during rewarming

rare.notes: Red/purple swollen lesions on digits after cold exposure

laboratory: ANA: negative (positive ANA suggests secondary Raynaud)
Specific antibodies (anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70, anti-U1 RNP): negative
imaging: Nailfold capillaroscopy: normal capillary architecture (abnormal in secondary Raynaud)
Digital plethysmography or laser Doppler: may confirm vasospasm
genetic: Familial clustering observed; no single causative gene
Possible association with NOS3, ADRA2C, and HIF1A gene polymorphisms
other: Cold provocation test: induces attacks under controlled conditions
Nailfold capillaroscopy is the single most important test to distinguish primary from secondary
Photo documentation of attacks helpful for diagnosis

distinguishingFeatures: Scleroderma has abnormal nailfold capillaroscopy (dilated loops, dropout)
Scleroderma has anti-centromere or anti-Scl-70 antibodies
Scleroderma may have skin thickening, digital pitting/ulcers
Erythromelalgia is triggered by heat (opposite of Raynaud)
Erythromelalgia has erythema and warmth, not pallor/cyanosis

redFlags: Asymmetric attacks (suggests vascular or structural cause)
Digital ulceration, pitting scars, or gangrene (strongly suggests secondary Raynaud/CTD)
Positive ANA or abnormal nailfold capillaroscopy (investigate for connective tissue disease)
Male sex with Raynaud (higher likelihood of secondary cause)
references: Wigley FM, Flavahan NA. Raynaud's Phenomenon. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(6):556-565.
Hughes M, Herrick AL. Raynaud's phenomenon. Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol. 2016;30(1):112-132.
Maverakis E, et al. International consensus criteria for the diagnosis of Raynaud's phenomenon. J Autoimmun. 2014;48-49:60-65.
